deep.reconstruction:
Context: This is a note in Gauss's electrodynamics material. The next page (205) treats 'Elektromotorische Kraft, durch Entstehung eines Stroms'. It computes ∫dx/r for a straight segment, log[(x'+√(x'²+y²))/(x0+√(x0²+y²))], and the inductance of a ring, 2M log(8R/(a e²)). So the 'Kraft' (X,Y,Z) here is the induction (electromotive) action of a closed current. In modern terms it is the vector potential of a unit current filament, Neumann's potential. The page explains a red marginal remark on p. 189.

(1) Setup. A closed curve C has points (x,y,z). The field point is (a,b,c), and r² = (x−a)²+(y−b)²+(z−c)². The force components are
X = ∮dx/r, Y = ∮dy/r, Z = ∮dz/r,
that is, A = ∮ ds/r. If C is plane with z constant, then dz = 0 and Z = 0.

(2) Definition of U. Write u = x−a, v = y−b, h = z−c (constant on a plane curve) and ρ² = u²+v². Gauss defines
U = ∮ r (u dv − v du)/ρ².
With tan λ = v/u, where λ is the azimuth of the curve point about the vertical through (a,b), we have dλ = (u dv − v du)/ρ². Hence U = ∮ r dλ.
In the margin he adds: if h = r sin θ (θ the elevation angle), then U = h ∮ dλ/sin θ.
A first attempt with a = b = 0, ∫(x dy − y dx) r/(x²+y²), is crossed out.

(3) Claim: X = ∂U/∂b and Y = −∂U/∂a.
Proof (mine; Gauss gives none). Let ω = P du + Q dv with P = −r v/ρ² and Q = r u/ρ². Then
∂Q/∂u − ∂P/∂v = div( r (u,v)/ρ² ) = (∇r·(u,v))/ρ² + r·div((u,v)/ρ²) = (ρ²/r)/ρ² + 0 = 1/r.
So dω = (1/r) du∧dv.
A shift of b is the flow −∂_v, so
∂U/∂b = −∮ L_{∂v} ω = −∮ [d(i_{∂v}ω) + i_{∂v}dω] = −∮ i_{∂v}dω = ∮ du/r = X.
In the same way, ∂U/∂a = −∮ L_{∂u} ω = −∮ i_{∂u}dω = −∮ dv/r = −Y.
Thus the planar vector potential is A = curl(U e_z), and U is a stream function.

(4) Consequence. Since (X,Y)·(∂U/∂a, ∂U/∂b) = U_b U_a − U_a U_b = 0 and Z = 0, the direction of (X,Y,Z) at every point lies in the surface U(a,b,c) = const. It also lies in the plane c = const. The field lines are therefore the intersections of these two surfaces, i.e. level curves of U in horizontal planes, and so they are closed ('kehrt in sich selbst zurück').
Gauss notes that this surface U = const differs from the surface V = const of p. 188. V is presumably the magnetic potential, the solid angle subtended by the circuit.
errors: No mathematical errors found. X = ∂U/∂b and Y = −∂U/∂a are correct for a closed plane curve.
The derivation is not written out; the step is stated without proof. It relies on div(r·(u,v)/ρ²) = 1/r and on the exact term vanishing around the closed curve.
Implicit restriction: the point (a,b) must not lie on the projection of the curve (ρ ≠ 0 along C), and c ≠ z unless the field point is off the curve.
Minor grammar: 'Die Richtungen ... fällt' (singular verb with plural noun).

results.what: Induction 'force' of a closed circuit written as the line integrals X = ∮dx/r, Y = ∮dy/r, Z = ∮dz/r
results.modern_name: Vector potential of a current filament (Neumann potential)
results.usually_credited_to: F. E. Neumann (1845/1847); later Kirchhoff, W. Weber, Maxwell

results.what: For a plane closed curve, (X,Y) = (∂U/∂b, −∂U/∂a) with U = ∮ r dλ = ∮ r((x−a)dy − (y−b)dx)/((x−a)²+(y−b)²)
results.modern_name: Stream function for the in-plane, divergence-free vector potential of a planar loop, A = curl(U e_z)
results.usually_credited_to: No specific attribution; the general idea is standard potential theory

results.what: Lines of the vector potential of a plane loop are closed curves: level sets of U in the planes c = const
results.modern_name: Field lines as level sets of a stream function

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss's unpublished electrodynamics notes from the 1830s–40s on induction are partly known (Werke V, Nachlass), and his anticipation of the vector-potential concept is discussed in the literature. The explicit stream function U = ∮ r dλ for a planar loop is a neat, correct, unpublished detail. Together with the next page (the ring inductance log(8R/a) − 2, usually attributed to Kirchhoff/Maxwell), it suggests a notable but not revolutionary anticipation of Neumann.

checkable.asserts: div(r·(u,v)/ρ²) = 1/r. Equals 0, which proves dω = du∧dv/r.

checkable.asserts: Numerically, ∂U/∂b = X = ∮dx/r for the unit circle in the plane z = 0, field point (0.3, −0.2, 0.5). Result ≈ 0.
Numerically, −∂U/∂a = Y = ∮dy/r for the same configuration. Result ≈ 0.
(X,Y)·∇U = 0, so the force direction is tangent to U = const.
